Setting upper and lower limits is a common control strategy but are frequently too generous to identify more subtle changes. Kernel density estimation (KDE) is a statistical method which estimates a probability density curve, most commonly as a normal or Gaussian distribution curve, which can identify extreme statistical outliers automatically as new data becomes available after manual tuning. Selection of an outlier removal method depends on the process. For example, negative values are impossible for most variables measured at WRRFs. Therefore, a strict threshold to replace negative values with “0” is appropriate. The most important consideration for an outlier detection method is automation. Can a set of rules be developed that, when always followed, will provide the best representation of the environmental and operational conditions? This set of rules will need to be automated for real-time deployment as new data is collected, and thus the manual approach or threshold approach may not be sustainable beyond the research phase of a project. Another frequently used data preparation method is imputation, which involves creating a predictive model for a single or multiple variables prior to ML model development. The model could be as simple as the arithmetic average or as complex as ML. For example, clustering algorithms like k nearest neighbors (KNN) uses a multivariate grouping approach and produces an average of those similar observations to impute missing data. However, it is important not to use future data when imputing if a method is to be used in real time, such as when doing linear interpolation between two points in time. When the model is deployed, the future value cannot be known and linear interpolation cannot be performed. Thus, the model training and testing errors may appear low in simulation, but without the incorporation of future information when deployed will perform poorly. This is an example of data leakage. In this case, interpolating using the ‘last known value’ is often used to best represent real world availability of laboratory values. Data imputation methods should both consider data availability and an accurate representation of the process. In the absence of information on how a process behaves between two time points, it is best to not impute and to either (1) exclude the variable due to infrequent data collection, (2) exclude the missing observation for all variables, or (3) use the last known value. Imputing in this case has been found to introduce more model error than resolve it (Newhart et al. 2021). It is important that data preparation be performed using data downloaded from the same process that will be used for deployment. For example, if the ML model will download data directly from the data historian using Python, then data for the preparation step should be downloaded directly from the data historian using Python.
